newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ex-Germany air cargo prices firm in Dec, some rise.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Germany air cargo prices firm in Dec, some rise.

text.p: Air cargo market rates out of Germany have firmed to most leading destinations as strong pre-Christmas demand outstrips available capacity, a Reuters' survey shows.
December business continued to reflect the pick-up in the export market seen in recent months, but several airlines said they had to turn away less cargo this year than at the end of previous years.
The main market feature was a last-minute rush to export goods, and machinery in particular, to China ahead of a January import tax rise, industry sources said.
The latest Frankfurt airport cargo figures show exports rose 6.4 percent in November and a similar rise is expected by market observers for December.
Forwarders are now gearing up to try to pass on to shippers a spate of early first quarter 1997 rates rises from leading carriers at a traditionally weak period of the year for cargo business.
Lufthansa Cargo will hike India prices by 15-70 percent from January 1 and introduce a general 7-10 percent price increase to selected destinations on March 1.
Air France will raise prices to India, Taiwan and Argentina on January 10 while KLM Royal Dutch Airlines is planning a 10-12 percent rates rise at some point in the first quarter.
British Airways will introduce several increases on January 1 ahead of a general increase towards the end of the first quarter.
Schenker International airfreight executive vice-president Klaus Geissler said: "The market is booming at present. Capacity is limited and the price situation is increasing upwards."
Business leading up to Christmas 1996 appeared to have been at similar levels to previous years with no significant changes, he added.
Air France Germany cargo director Helmut Scherret said: "Export figures are very good at present and we are optimistic that this will continue."
Cargo manager Central Europe, Mark Gardiner, said BA business in Germany was a little weak in December but volumes were good on core routes such as the North Atlantic.
The Asian market in December was strongly influenced by the surge in demand for China, which increased market rates to Hong Kong and Shanghai due to a capacity shortage, sources said.
Lufthansa Cargo said it saw a rise in shipments from companies such as Volkswagen AG and Siemens AG on its freighter services from Frankfurt to Shanghai and Beijing.
Frank Wortmann, managing director of Air China sales agent Penta Shipping, said: "China is booming. At the moment everyone is trying to get everything into China."
Cargo volumes on the weekly joint freighter service with Lufthansa were good and slightly up on last year, he added.
Dieter Uhl, managing director of Air Impact, sales agent for China Eastern, which flies twice-weekly from Munich to Shanghai with a passenger-configuration Airbus 340, said cargo capacity was full.
"Demand for China is going very strongly. There is tremendous pressure in the last few days of December because capacity is not there and so full charters are going out," he added.
Several cargo charters had been organised from Luxemburg and Ostend to beat the December 31 customs fee deadline, he noted.
KLM Central Europe sales director, Oliver Evans, said: "There is huge demand for China. Demand is channelled through Hong Kong and is very high, and I anticipate this trend will continue."
The two key Far East markets, Japan and Korea, continued to show strong demand in December, allowing higher yields to be achieved.
Korean Air Germany sales manager, Robert M. Instinsky, said: "December was very, very good, especially for business to China and south-east Asia."
Rival Korean carrier, Asiana Airlines, claims it is gaining business in Germany although it flies at present only a twice-weekly ex-Brussels Boeing 747 combi service.
Lothar Schaller, sales manager of Aerotrans, the airline's Germany gsa, said "The carrier is being accepted very well by the forwarders and the market to Seoul is very good.
"Korea is booming and I think that will continue in the medium-term. We could do with more capacity as it is very limited at present," he added.
But the launch of twice-weekly Boeing 747 combi flights between Seoul and Frankfurt from next May would allow a more active sales strategy, he noted.
Rates to India will soar from January 1 from the current 1.60-1.70 marks per kg levels following the decision of Lufthansa Cargo, Air India, Air France and KLM to increase prices dramatically.

Air India cargo services manager, Wolfgang Scholinz, said demand for the sub-continent out of Germany was very strong but freight operations were financially hit at present by low rates generated by over-capacity.
Market rates to North America have risen by several pfennigs in December as demand increased relative to the substantial belly cargo capacity in the market.
Delta Air Lines cargo sales representative Manfred Schleiffer said: "Business is very busy and we are booked out to all destinations."
U.S. carriers had been able to plan their December cargo allocations better this year under a new agreement on military mail traffic with the U.S. Post Office, he noted.

Through a fixed rotation system for mail, each airline knew from the start of December how many mail containers it would have to take up to Christmas and thus how much empty cargo space was available, Schleiffer explained.
TWA cargo sales manager Petra Lentes added: "Business is going very well at present and flights are full."
The Christmas military mail was a major revenue-earner at the moment, she added.
USAir was achieving an ex-Germany load factor of more than 90 percent on its daily Frankfurt flights at present, Lothar Schaller, sales manager of Germany gsa Aerotrans, said.
KLM's Evans noted: "The North American market is recovering after a period of slight growth."
This had enabled the airline to raise U.S. rates from October but rates remained generally at very competitive levels, he said.
Air France's Scherret added: "We are in a phase where the rates level is stabilising and slowly increasing."
"There is a lot of competition from belly carriers who have very low rates, too low in our opinion," he added.
Market rates to Latin America are rising slightly as European carriers such as Air France and Iberia increase prices.
Iberia Germany sales manager George von Doehren said the airline had put up ex-Germany rates to all Latin American destinations by 10 pfennigs on December 1.
"Our rates were perhaps not the highest, the resonance was positive and there were no complaints," he said.
"Business is very good at present but we are not having to turn down so much at present. There is a little less demand but we could do with more space allotments."
Demand in Germany for Buenos Aires was continuing to grow strongly while Santiago and Lima were developing well, he noted.
Air France will raise rates to Buenos Aires, which it serves with a twice weekly ex-Paris freighter, from January 10.
The airline's Germany cargo director, Helmut Scherret, said: "The market for South America is good. Imports are growing there."
The key Brazilian market has continued to grow strongly recently but January and early February are likely to be quieter due to the Carnival festivities, industry sources said.
Import demand is expected to be boosted as imports at airports are speeded up by a new computerised customs system from January 2, they added.
The Ciscomix system will register imports on computer, reduce paperwork and ease processing of foreign trade with Brazil, they noted.
Rates to the main African market, South Africa, have remained stable in December, sources said.

South African Airways (SAA.CN) Germany sales manager Hugo Duchemin said business for the airline's three times a week joint freighter service with Lufthansa Cargo had been good from October through to mid-December. "We have been able to stop the yield fall and our market share is satisfactory," he said.
He criticised European carriers who offered transshipment rates of 3.80-3.50 marks per kg since freight tonnage was sufficient for niche carriers to earn at higher rates.

Air Namibia, which flies Frankfurt via Windhoek to Johannesburg three times a week, has a cargo load factor of 85 percent at present after a market improvement in the autumn, its Germany gsa Aerotrans said.

Aerotrans sales manager Germany, Lothar Schaller, said: "Because the Namibian market is so small we have specialised on the South African market. Freight is not unloaded in Windhoek and there is only a two-hour stop, so it is nearly a direct flight." - Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
